abstract: In dynamic environments where rewards continuously change, adaptive decision-making requires ongoing updates of option-value and uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. This process depends on cognitive resources and involves coordinated interactions among multiple brain regions; however, how cognitive load affects directed exploration in such dynamic environments, and whether these effects are accompanied by changes in interactions among exploration-related brain regions, remains unclear. We embedded a working-memory load manipulation within a dynamic four-armed bandit task. Experiment 1 compared computational models and quantified load-related changes in exploration; Experiment 2 examined these behavioral effects in an independent sample and investigated their neural correlates using fMRI. Across both experiments, high load reduced the uncertainty bonus parameter ({varphi}), indicating weaker directed exploration. Experiment 2 additionally showed lower inverse temperature ({beta}) under high load, indicating more stochastic choices. Directed exploration relative to exploitation more activated the frontopolar cortex (FP), intraparietal sulcus (IPS), anterior insula (aIns), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses indicated stronger functional coupling between the right aIns and IPS under low load. Guided by the candidate connections identified by PPI, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) focused on a three-region subnetwork. Bayesian model selection favored the model with directed-exploration-related input to the IPS, while condition-specific comparisons suggested stronger aIns-to-IPS effective connectivity under low load. Together, these findings link cognitive resource demands to reduced uncertainty-guided directed exploration in a dynamic environment and suggest that this behavioral change is accompanied by selective reconfiguration of interactions within an IPS-centered decision subnetwork.
